b) Visual Impact of, and From, the Site. With the expressed objective of making the prototype sites demonstrations of good planning and design, it was generally considered that the completed sites would enhance the neighborhood. Consideration was given to site design aspects where the visual environment from outside the site would detract or enhance the livability in the site. Two examples will suffice: At Jersey City, many of the housing units on this site will have a direct view of lower Manhattan and the New York harbor area; building arrangements were designed to maximize this aspect of the site. On the other hand, at Kalamazoo, there is an apartment development immediately adjacent to the site which is poorly planned and not particularly attractive; in this instance, the site planner designed a visual barrier of trees to minimize the negative aspects of this exposure.
c) Housing Densities and Open Space: All of the site planners developed cluster planning schemes, whereby total housing densities could be increased above normal levels while still providing improved open space for recreation and livability requirements. In general, consideration was given to a separation of vehicular and pedestrian traffic, defining pedestrian paths to the various community facilities. The planners also studied the visual impact of various housing systems as they related to each other and to the total site design.
d) <u>Utility Development</u>: Good planning can not only reduce the unit cost of land to a housing unit; it can also reduce the per unit cost of utilities. The site utility systems were carefully designed to make full use of the cluster concept. In addition, innovations such as common trenching were tried where appropriate.
As a general rule, utility services were obtained from the local community. In every case, water is supplied by the local water company or department, and sanitary sewers (which are separate from storm sewers) tie into city systems. Where city storm drainage existed, it was utilized. However, two sites, Kalamazoo and Macon, abut lakes and two others utilize surface drainage for storm water runoff (Indianapolis and King County); these sites received special attention, as noted under "Special Site Features", below.
Natural gas was available to every site, except that availability in Jersey City was limited to individual dwelling units for cooking purposes only. Generally (but not universally), the housing systems producers selected gas for their heating system energy source. A few systems have been designed to use electrical heating and cooling equipment. Electrical power distribution is underground on every site, supplied from the local power company on all sites except Jersey City. Jersey City is providing a test for total energy and pneumatic trash collection systems, as described below:
Solid waste management has also been an important factor in the design of the sites. The Environmental Protection Agency evaluated each of the sites relative to proposed methods for solid waste handling, and reviewed commercially-available equipment for this purpose. A report covering this evaluation, now in preparation, is expected to be generally useful in planning any new development.
